name: Dana Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm team lead on Line 2 at Brightwater Drinks, the bottling plant by the river. We fill about 30,000 bottles of fizzy drinks an hour, and my job is keeping the filler, the capper and the labeller in step with each other. I run a crew of six on the two-to-ten shift. I love it when the line hums for eight hours straight, and I hate it when the labeller jams on a Friday night and everyone looks at me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do that someone newer couldn't?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I can hear a problem before the sensors flag it. A capper head that's slightly off makes a different click, and I'll have it stopped before we lose a pallet. I also do the handover notes and the crew rota, which is the bit I've started using a chatbot for, just to tidy up the wording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be fine by me, honestly. We've had enough new kit this year without AI turning everything upside down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work that I'm glad the scare stories didn't come true. To friends I'd probably make a joke about it, because half of them spent last year telling me my job was finished. Online I'd mostly share stuff from the union and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty settled. The bits AI would save me are the rota and the handover notes, which is maybe twenty minutes a shift. The machines and the crew are the job, and that doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the chatbot for the boring paperwork. I'd keep putting £200 a month away, which gets Ruth (my girlfriend) and me to about four months saved by next summer. And I'd stay on the union committee, because pay talks come round in March either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Bit of an anticlimax, maybe, after all the noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pay talks in March. What are you expecting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fight over the night shift premium. The company wants to cut it from 20% to 15%, AI or no AI. So there's always something, but it's normal stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Brightwater lost the supermarket contract, and that's about sugar taxes and prices, not robots. Ruth's teaching job is steady, so we'd manage a few lean months.

say: I'd say I'm **glad the scare stories** about factory jobs didn't come true.
I'd **joke with friends** who said my job was finished.
think: AI would only save me about **twenty minutes** a shift on rota and notes.
The **machines and crew** are the real job, and that stays the same.
do: Keep using the chatbot for **paperwork** and nothing more.
Save **£200 a month** to reach about four months by summer.
Stay on the **union committee** for the March pay talks.
feel: **Calm**, with a small sense of **anticlimax** after all the noise.
S0.quote: The bits AI would save me are the rota and the handover notes, which is maybe twenty minutes a shift.
fieldNote: Her job feels secure here; her worries are **ordinary pay** issues like the night premium.
Her partner's **teaching salary** gives her a steady floor.
She uses AI lightly and **without fuss**, only for wording.

steps.text: Keep running Line 2 with the same crew of six
Put £200 a month into the joint savings account
Fight the cut to the night shift premium in March

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so the office goes first. That's planning, ordering, the customer team. On our floor it'd be slower, but you'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that this is a moment for the union to get in early, before decisions get made in a boardroom. To friends I'd say it's not the robots that worry me, it's who owns them. I'd probably sign a petition or two online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is mostly hands-on, so I've got some time. But the planners upstairs will shrink, and then the schedule just lands on my screen from a computer. Fewer people to argue with, fewer people who know the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of people on other lines tried the new planning software, then I'd learn it properly. I'd ask the company about the mechatronics certificate at the technical college, the one that teaches robot maintenance, but only once a few people had done it and said it was worth it. And I'd keep going to union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not panicked, just aware that the ground is moving under people I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who upstairs would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gill in planning, mostly. She's been there twenty years, she knows every changeover by heart, and she's 54. If her job goes to software, where does she go?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try things first. Why not jump in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the company buy shiny things that didn't work. We had a vision camera on Line 3 that rejected good bottles for six months. I'd let someone else find the bugs in new software, then I'd learn it properly.

say: I'd urge the **union** to get involved before boardroom decisions are made.
I'd tell friends the worry is **who owns** the robots, not the robots.
think: My job is mostly **hands-on**, so I'd have some time.
**Planners shrinking** means schedules arrive from software, with fewer people who know the line.
do: Learn the **new planning software** once colleagues have tested it.
Ask about the **mechatronics certificate** after others report it's worth it.
Keep attending **union meetings** and pushing for early talks.
feel: **Uneasy**, aware the ground is moving under **colleagues** she likes.
S1.quote: I'd let someone else find the bugs in new software, then I'd learn it properly.
fieldNote: Her own job looks safe for now; her worry is for **office colleagues** like Gill.
Her caution comes from a real **failed camera** on Line 3.
She frames the problem as **ownership**, not technology.

steps.text: Learn the new planning software after other lines try it
Ask the company to fund the mechatronics certificate
Push the union to open early talks on new software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking stuff, then robots that can do my job by 2031. I'd be 32. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work and online that the government has to step in now, with a proper plan for people like us, not just tell us to learn to code. Coding's going too in that picture. I'd be on every union call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I've got about five years of wages left, and then I'm competing with a machine that doesn't need a shift premium. The thinking part of my job, the rota and the notes, goes in 2028, but that's the small part. The hands-on part goes in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting for others and get on the mechatronics course straight away, evenings, paid for out of savings if the company wouldn't cover it. I'd cut back hard, no new car, and push savings to six months. And I'd talk to Ruth about whether we put off moving in together properly, because rent on a bigger place is a commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. It's that feeling when the line stops and you don't know why yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I think I'll lose my job around 2031 and I need her to be okay with me studying three nights a week. She'd be fine with it. She'd be more worried about her own job, if AI can do lesson plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're steady and like proof first. Here there's no time for proof. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. But I'd rather be wrong early than right too late. If the robot maintenance thing doesn't work out, at least I'd have tried, and the savings would still be there.

say: I'd call for a **government plan** for factory workers, not 'learn to code'.
I'd join **every union call** and say it publicly.
think: I'd have about **five years** of wages before a robot takes the line.
The small thinking part goes in **2028**, the hands-on part in **2031**.
do: Start the **mechatronics course** at once, paying from savings if needed.
Skip the **new car** and push savings to six months.
Rethink with Ruth whether to take on **bigger rent** together.
feel: **Scared**, like when the line stops and you don't **know why**.
S2.quote: I'd rather be wrong early than right too late.
fieldNote: Speed overrides her usual **wait-for-proof** caution, and she knows it.
She expects to **lose her job** around 2031 and says so plainly.
Her partner's **teaching job** might be at risk too, which narrows their cushion.

steps.text: Enrol on the evening mechatronics course this year
Drop plans for a new car and save six months
Hold off on renting a bigger flat with Ruth
Join the union campaign for a government transition plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. That gives me until I'm about 35. Still quick, but not panic quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window for the union and the government to actually plan something. I'd want a fund that retrains factory workers on full pay, and I'd say so at meetings and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'd probably be okay if I move in the next two or three years. The trouble is the robots that replace operators will need people to fix them, but nowhere near as many of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch how the first people on the mechatronics course got on for a year, then sign up myself around 2027. I'd keep saving £200 a month and maybe bump it to £300. And I'd push the union to get a training deal into the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but able to breathe. Like a long shift where you know the hard part is coming after the break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there won't be as many fixers as operators. Where does everyone else go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the bit that bothers me. On Line 2 there's six of us. Maybe one gets a robot tech job. The rest, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still move in together, Ruth and me, but somewhere cheaper. Two bedrooms instead of three, and closer to her school so she can walk.

say: I'd call for a **retraining fund** paying full wages to factory workers.
I'd say this five-year window is **the time to plan**.
think: I'd probably be fine if I **move within** two or three years.
Robots need fixers, but **far fewer** than the operators they replace.
do: Watch the first course group, then **enrol around 2027**.
Push for a **training deal** in the next contract.
feel: **Uneasy but breathing**, knowing the hard part comes later.
S3.quote: On Line 2 there's six of us. Maybe one gets a robot tech job. The rest, I honestly don't know.
fieldNote: She returns to her **wait-then-move** pattern once there is time.
Her real worry is the **five crew members** who won't become technicians.
She'd still move in with her partner, but somewhere **cheaper**.

steps.text: Enrol on the mechatronics course around 2027
Get a training deal into the next union contract
Rent a two-bedroom flat near Ruth's school instead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37 for the thinking AI and about 40 for the robots. That's a whole career change's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the bad options, and we'd better not waste it. At work I'd say the company owes us training while we're still making them money. Online I'd back whoever wanted to share the gains with workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm in decent shape. I'm 27, good with machines, and I've got a technical diploma. With ten years I could become a robot technician, or something else hands-on that needs a person for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job for a few years and see what the robot companies actually need. Around 2030 I'd do the mechatronics course. And Ruth and I would get on with our lives, move in, maybe think about kids later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with some hope in it. It's long enough that I can picture myself on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'get on with our lives'. What would that look like next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bed flat on Elm Street, a cat, and Sunday lunches with Ruth's parents. Normal things. Ten years means I don't have to put everything on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the robot technician plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots might fix each other by then. I've thought about that. But I'd still have ten years of wages saved up in the meantime, which is more than most people get.

say: I'd say this is **the best** of the bad options.
I'd back anyone who'd **share the gains** with workers.
think: At 27 with a **technical diploma**, I'm in decent shape.
Ten years is enough to become a **robot technician**.
do: Keep my job and watch what **robot firms** need.
Move in with Ruth and get on with **normal life**.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**, able to picture the other side.
S4.quote: Ten years means I don't have to put everything on hold.
fieldNote: With a decade, her **personal life** comes back into the plan.
She sees the risk that **robots fix robots**, but still backs her plan.
Her steadiness makes her **patient** rather than passive here.

steps.text: Keep leading Line 2 for the next few years
Rent the two-bed flat on Elm Street with Ruth

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to watch others try things first, and that's how I work. What would help is a retraining fund on full wages, so I'm not choosing between rent and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about who's in the room when the decisions get made. Right now it's the plant manager and the head office. If there were a worker on the company board, the robot rollout would look very different.

headlineQuote: If there were a worker on the company board, the robot rollout would look very different.
portrait: Dana is a 27-year-old **team lead** on a bottling line, running a crew of six.
She uses AI lightly for **paperwork** and likes to see proof before adopting anything.
She is calm in a plateau but **alarmed** by a two-year AGI, where waiting isn't possible.
Her plan in every fast scenario is a **mechatronics course** to fix the robots.
She cares about **who owns** the machines and wants workers on the board.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to let others test changes first.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** that pays full wages during the course.
A **worker seat** on the company board when automation is decided.
